catalog_quote: As common in Bantu, Cuwabo has a binary tone system, intertwining high (H) and toneless (Ø) pitches. In this study, H tones are indicated by means of an acute accent. [...] The tone-bearing unit in Cuwabo is the mora, which represents the smallest phonological unit in a syllabic nucleus (Hayes 1989, Hyman 1992). [...] The great majority of Cuwabo words have at least one primary H tone [...]. In fact, only a few grammatical words (e.g. akala 'if') and ideophones can have an all-low tone pattern. new_statements.quote: As common in Bantu, Cuwabo has a binary tone system, intertwining high (H) and toneless (Ø) pitches. [...] The tone-bearing unit in Cuwabo is the mora, which represents the smallest phonological unit in a syllabic nucleus [...] (p. 86) [...] Finally, unlike many eastern Bantu languages such as Chewa, Swahili, Mwani (Devos 2008), Makonde (Manus 2003, Kraal 2005), Cuwabo is not subject to penultimate lengthening at the end of a prosodic unit (although the falling H may be viewed as reminiscent of a system formerly marked by penultimate lengthening, as already stated above). (p. 88)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Cuwabo is described purely as a tone language (privative H vs Ø, mora as TBU, lexical and grammatical tone, tonal minimal pairs); the grammar makes no statement about word stress or accent and explicitly denies the phrase-penultimate lengthening typical of eastern Bantu. The only positional regularities are tonal: every word surfaces with at least one H, underlyingly toneless nouns receive a predictable H on the second mora of the word (first stem mora after a prefix), and a doubled H landing on the penult of a prosodic unit is realised as a falling tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (no stress analysis at all).
new_statements.exceptions: A few grammatical words (e.g. akala 'if') and ideophones may be all-low. The author notes (p. 22) that the 1989 orthography standardisation report claimed general penultimate vowel lengthening ('todas as vogais sofrem um alongamento, geralmente na penúltima sílaba') and rejects this as not attested synchronically; the penult falling contour (p. 86) is offered as a possible relic of former penultimate lengthening.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone patterns given for citation forms (nouns uttered sentence-finally); the falling realisation of a doubled H and the (absent) lengthening are stated for the right edge of a prosodic unit/phrase, not the word. Section 3.6.3 treats extra-high pitch on certain moras as intonational 'rhetorical emphasis', not lexical stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Guérois 2015 is explicitly based on central Cuwabo, the variety spoken around Quelimane and Macuse (Zambezia), as opposed to the Karungu, Mayindo, Marale/Manyawa and Nyaringa dialects (thesis p. ~10-11). Same language as Glottolog chuw1238 / ISO chw (spelled Chuwabu, Chuwabo, Cuwabo, Ecuwabo, Echuwabo, Txuwabo, Xuabo).

new_statements.quote: Ecuwabo closely parallels Emakhuwa in its tonology. There are two basic tones, High and Low. H tones (whatever their source) double onto the following mora, but like many Emakhuwa dialects, this doubling cannot affect a phrase-final vowel. Furthermore tone spreading is found in Ecuwabo, unlike Emakhuwa where it is unusual. [...] As in some Emakhuwa varieties, a doubled H on a phrase-penult mora is realized with a falling character: w-aábâla 'to wear clothes' versus w-aábálela 'to dress well'. (p. 195) [...] In the absence of a MH, a lexical H tone emerges on the penult mora of the stem (or the ultimate mora in the case of a bimoraic stem), while low stems remain toneless. (p. 196)
new_statements.citation: Kisseberth, Charles W. & Rozenn Guérois. 2014. Melodic H tones in Emakhuwa and Ecuwabo verbs. Africana Linguistica 20: 181-205.

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing statement from Guérois 2015 (binary H/toneless tone system, mora as TBU, no stress statement, doubled H on the phrase-penult realised falling). The catalog record for Cuwabo has an empty rule; this article supports keeping it as a tone language with no word-stress rule. It adds tone detail (lexical H/L verb-root contrast retained, four melodic-H patterns, tone bridges) but nothing on stress, penultimate lengthening or any other culminative prominence.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The article is a study of melodic (grammatical) H tone in verbs. For Ecuwabo it states a two-tone (H vs L/toneless) mora-based tone system with rightward H doubling (blocked on a phrase-final vowel), tone spreading, a falling realisation of a doubled H on the phrase-penult mora, and a retained lexical H/toneless contrast on verb roots (lexical H surfacing on the stem penult, or the final mora of bimoraic stems). The words 'stress', 'prominence' and 'lengthening' do not occur anywhere in the text; 'accent' occurs once, only as the name of the acute diacritic marking surface H (p. 182). No word-stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Tone: MH cannot double onto a phrase-final vowel (pp. 195, 199); MS1 melodic H retracts to the preceding mora/prefix when the stem carries a lexical H or when the target would be word-final (pp. 199-201); longer verb stems sometimes neutralise the H/L lexical contrast (p. 196 n. 6).
new_statements.identity_note: The article's Ecuwabo data are the authors' own fieldwork on Ecuwabo 'classified as P34 by Guthrie, and spoken in the South of Zambezia province' (p. 195); no sub-dialect is named. It treats Ecuwabo as a 'mixed-Emakhuwa' language (Emakhuwa P30 morphology with a Zone N component, p. 182, p. 196). Most of the article (sections 1-2, pp. 182-195) concerns Emakhuwa dialects (Ikorovere, Esaaka, Eeratti, Imitthupi, Ilê, Imeetto, Enahara, Rovuma), not Cuwabo.
